lessonTitle: Purine Degradation, Uric Acid and Gout

blocks.text: A 52-year-old man is woken at 3 a.m. by a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender big toe that cannot bear the weight of the bedsheet. The night before he enjoyed a large meal of liver and several beers. A joint aspirate shows needle-shaped crystals engulfed by neutrophils. The crystals are sodium urate, the end product of purine breakdown in humans, and this unit explains how they form and how a drug can prevent them.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** Nucleic acids and nucleotides are constantly turned over, and the purine bases (adenine and guanine) cannot be oxidised further to CO2 in humans. Instead their rings are degraded to a single poorly soluble end product, **uric acid**, which is excreted mostly in urine. If production exceeds excretion, plasma urate rises (**hyperuricaemia**) and may crystallise in joints, causing gout.

**Tracing the pathway.** Adenine nucleotides: AMP is converted to adenosine (by 5'-nucleotidase) or to IMP (by AMP deaminase). Adenosine is deaminated to **inosine** by **adenosine deaminase (ADA)**. **Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)** cleaves inosine to **hypoxanthine** and ribose-1-phosphate. Guanine nucleotides: GMP is converted to **guanosine**, cleaved by PNP to **guanine**, which is deaminated to **xanthine** by guanine deaminase. Finally **xanthine oxidase** converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to **uric acid**, a molybdenum-containing enzyme that generates hydrogen peroxide. Every purine ring becomes one molecule of uric acid.

rows: AMP deaminase or 5'-nucleotidase, then adenosine deaminase
blocks.caption: Purine catabolism to uric acid. Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency and PNP deficiency causes T-cell immunodeficiency.

blocks.title: How much uric acid from a nucleotide load?
blocks.prompt: Cell death releases 0.010 mol of AMP, all of which is degraded to uric acid (molar mass 168 g per mole). What mass of uric acid is formed?

steps.text: Each AMP contains one purine ring, which ends as one uric acid molecule, so 0.010 mol of AMP gives 0.010 mol of uric acid.
Mass = moles x molar mass = 0.010 x 168 g = 1.68 g.

blocks.answer: 1.68 g of uric acid. This is comparable to the whole body urate pool, which is why large nucleotide loads can precipitate hyperuricaemia.

blocks.markdown: **Why humans make urate, and why it precipitates.** Most mammals have **uricase (urate oxidase)**, which converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin; humans have lost this enzyme. Uric acid is a weak acid (pKa about 5.8), so at the pH of blood it exists mainly as the sodium salt **monosodium urate**, whose solubility in plasma at body temperature is only about 0.42 mmol per litre (about 7 mg per decilitre). Above this level plasma is supersaturated. In acid urine (low pH) uric acid itself is poorly soluble and can form kidney stones.

rows: High cell turnover (leukaemia, chemotherapy-induced tumour lysis), HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan), PRPP synthetase overactivity, high-purine diet, alcohol and fructose
Chronic kidney disease, thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, lactic acidosis, ketosis, dehydration
blocks.caption: Causes of hyperuricaemia. Both mechanisms often coexist.

blocks.markdown: **Allopurinol.** Allopurinol is a structural analogue of hypoxanthine. It is oxidised by xanthine oxidase to **oxypurinol (alloxanthine)**, which binds tightly to the enzyme and inhibits it. Purine breakdown therefore stops at **hypoxanthine and xanthine**, which are much more soluble than urate and are excreted. Plasma urate and urinary uric acid fall. Because it blocks the enzyme, allopurinol also slows the breakdown of the purine-based drugs azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, whose toxicity can rise (a pharmacology teaching point; doses are adjusted by specialists).

blocks.title: Allopurinol and purine-based drugs
blocks.text: Xanthine oxidase inactivates 6-mercaptopurine (the active product of azathioprine). Combining these with allopurinol can cause dangerous bone-marrow toxicity unless doses are reduced under specialist supervision. This is stated as a pharmacology teaching example, not as advice.

blocks.markdown: **Pathogenesis of gout.** Persistent hyperuricaemia leads to deposition of **monosodium urate crystals** in joints (classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint, called podagra) and soft tissue. In an acute attack, crystals shed into the joint are phagocytosed by macrophages and neutrophils, activating the **NLRP3 inflammasome**, which releases **interleukin-1 beta**; this recruits neutrophils and causes the hot, red, painful joint. Under polarised light the crystals are **needle-shaped and negatively birefringent** (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). With long-standing disease, crystal masses form **tophi** in cartilage, tendons and ears, and chronic joint damage, and uric acid stones may occur. Acute attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory agents such as NSAIDs or colchicine; long-term urate-lowering therapy is started after the attack settles.

blocks.title: Converting a laboratory urate result
blocks.prompt: A laboratory reports serum urate as 7.0 mg per decilitre. Convert it to micromol per litre (molar mass 168 g per mole).
blocks.answer: About 417 micromol per litre, close to the saturation limit of monosodium urate.

blocks.title: Where allopurinol acts
blocks.text: Allopurinol blocks the last two steps (hypoxanthine to xanthine, xanthine to uric acid). Hypoxanthine and xanthine accumulate and are excreted, while urate falls. It does not reduce the inflammation of an acute attack and may even provoke an attack when first started.

points: Purine nucleotides are degraded via inosine, hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid by xanthine oxidase; humans lack uricase.
Hyperuricaemia arises from overproduction or, more commonly, reduced renal excretion, and monosodium urate saturates at about 0.42 mmol per litre.
Allopurinol (through oxypurinol) inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering urate and raising the more soluble hypoxanthine and xanthine.
Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals that activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release; the crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the last two steps of purine degradation, converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid?

options.text: Xanthine oxidase
Adenosine deaminase
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase
Uricase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: xanthine oxidase oxidises hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid.
distractorRationale.b: Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine, earlier in the pathway.
distractorRationale.c: PNP cleaves inosine and guanosine to the free bases, before the oxidation steps.
distractorRationale.d: Uricase converts uric acid to allantoin and is absent in humans.

questions.explanation: After the bases hypoxanthine and guanine-derived xanthine are formed, xanthine oxidase performs the final oxidations to uric acid. It is the target of allopurinol.

questions.stem: Why is uric acid, rather than allantoin, the end product of purine degradation in humans?

options.text: Humans lack uricase (urate oxidase)
Humans lack xanthine oxidase
Humans lack adenosine deaminase
Purine rings cannot be degraded in any species

distractorRationale.a: Correct: uricase converts urate to the more soluble allantoin in most mammals but is absent in humans.
distractorRationale.b: Humans have xanthine oxidase; it is how uric acid is made.
distractorRationale.c: ADA is present; its deficiency causes immunodeficiency, not the lack of an end product.
distractorRationale.d: Purine rings are degraded further in many mammals, just not in humans.

questions.explanation: Uricase oxidises uric acid to allantoin, which is soluble and excreted. Humans have lost the functional gene, so uric acid remains as the final product and is poorly soluble.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent gout is started on allopurinol. Which change in plasma purine metabolites would be expected?

options.text: Urate falls while hypoxanthine and xanthine rise
Urate rises while hypoxanthine and xanthine fall
All three fall because purine synthesis is blocked
Urate falls because allantoin is formed

questions.correctOptionText: Urate falls while hypoxanthine and xanthine rise

distractorRationale.a: Correct: xanthine oxidase inhibition blocks formation of urate and the more soluble precursors accumulate.
distractorRationale.b: This would happen if xanthine oxidase were more active, not inhibited.
distractorRationale.c: Allopurinol acts on degradation, not on de novo synthesis, and the precursors increase.
distractorRationale.d: Humans do not make allantoin because they lack uricase.

questions.explanation: Oxypurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme making urate from hypoxanthine and xanthine. These precursors therefore build up, but they are more soluble than urate and are excreted, lowering the risk of crystal formation.

questions.stem: Polarised light microscopy of synovial fluid from an acutely inflamed joint shows crystals engulfed by neutrophils. Which finding identifies the crystals as monosodium urate?

options.text: Needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringence
Rhomboid crystals with weakly positive birefringence
Hexagonal plates of cholesterol
Apple-green birefringence after Congo red staining

distractorRationale.a: Correct: monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.
distractorRationale.b: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals are typical of calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout).
distractorRationale.c: Cholesterol crystals are plates and are not the typical gout finding.
distractorRationale.d: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red identifies amyloid, not urate.

questions.explanation: Urate crystals are needle-like and show strong negative birefringence under compensated polarised light. Finding them within neutrophils in an acutely inflamed joint confirms gout.

questions.stem: A woman with inflammatory bowel disease on azathioprine develops a severe fall in white cell count after her doctor adds allopurinol for hyperuricaemia. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine, so the active drug accumulates
Allopurinol stimulates purine synthesis and raises 6-mercaptopurine
Allopurinol converts azathioprine to uric acid
Allopurinol inhibits adenosine deaminase, causing immunodeficiency

questions.correctOptionText: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine, so the active drug accumulates

distractorRationale.a: Correct: xanthine oxidase degrades 6-mercaptopurine; blocking it raises levels and marrow toxicity.
distractorRationale.b: Allopurinol does not stimulate purine synthesis.
distractorRationale.c: Azathioprine is not converted to uric acid.
distractorRationale.d: Allopurinol does not inhibit adenosine deaminase.

questions.explanation: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which is partly inactivated by xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol blocks this pathway so more drug is available, causing bone-marrow suppression unless the dose is reduced; this is a pharmacology teaching example.

questions.stem: True or false: uric acid is more soluble in acidic urine than in alkaline urine.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Uric acid is a weak acid with a pKa around 5.8. In acid urine it is mainly the un-ionised, poorly soluble form that can crystallise into stones, whereas at higher pH it is converted to the more soluble urate.

questions.stem: A patient's laboratory report gives serum urate as 8.4 mg per decilitre. Using a molar mass of 168 g per mole, convert this to micromol per litre.
questions.explanation: 8.4 mg/dL = 84 mg/L = 0.084 g/L. Dividing by 168 g/mol gives 0.0005 mol/L = 0.50 mmol/L = 500 micromol/L. This is above the approximate saturation point of monosodium urate (about 420 micromol per litre), so crystallisation risk is increased.

questions.stem: Chemotherapy for leukaemia lyses cells and releases 0.030 mol of purine nucleotides, all of which are degraded to uric acid (molar mass 168 g per mole, one uric acid per purine ring). What mass of uric acid is formed?
questions.explanation: Each purine ring is degraded to one molecule of uric acid, so 0.030 mol of nucleotide gives 0.030 mol of uric acid. Mass = 0.030 x 168 = 5.04 g, several times the normal body urate pool, which explains tumour lysis hyperuricaemia and the use of urate-lowering measures.

questions.stem: Trace the degradation of adenine and guanine nucleotides to uric acid, naming the key enzymes and intermediates.
markingGuide: AMP to adenosine (or IMP), then adenosine deaminase gives inosine
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase converts inosine to hypoxanthine
GMP to guanosine, then PNP gives guanine
Guanine deaminase converts guanine to xanthine
Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid
Uric acid is the final product in humans and is excreted in urine because humans lack uricase
questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine nucleotides take different routes but converge at xanthine, which is oxidised to uric acid by xanthine oxidase. The two pathways can be remembered by the key enzymes ADA, PNP, guanine deaminase and xanthine oxidase.

questions.stem: Explain the pathogenesis of acute gouty arthritis, from hyperuricaemia to joint inflammation, and explain how allopurinol reduces the risk of attacks.
markingGuide: Sustained hyperuricaemia above the solubility of monosodium urate (about 0.42 mmol per litre) from overproduction or underexcretion
Crystallisation of monosodium urate in joints, e.g. first metatarsophalangeal joint, and soft tissue (tophi)
Crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages and neutrophils, activating the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release
Neutrophil recruitment causing acute hot, red, swollen, painful joint
Crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent on polarised light microscopy
Allopurinol (oxypurinol) inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering urate production and raising more soluble hypoxanthine and xanthine
Lower urate prevents crystal formation and allows existing crystals to dissolve over time
questions.explanation: Gout is a crystal-induced inflammatory arthritis that depends on urate exceeding its solubility. Allopurinol treats the cause by lowering urate production, whereas anti-inflammatory drugs treat the attack itself.
